name: Unbounded queries
summary: A query with no time range, no partition key and no LIMIT, whose cost grows with every row ever stored.
howItWorks: A query is bounded when something in it caps how much data the database must touch: a time range, a partition or primary key, or a LIMIT that an index can satisfy. Leave all of them out and the database has to read everything, so a query that took 20 ms in the first week takes minutes a year later with no code changed. Time-series data makes this worse because it only grows. Common culprits are a dashboard panel set to “all time”, a Grafana SQL panel without the `$__timeFilter()` macro, `SELECT *` on a hypertable with no `WHERE time > ...`, a PromQL range covering months, a DynamoDB `Scan` (which reads every item, and charges for every item even when a filter drops most of them), a Cassandra query with `ALLOW FILTERING`, and page 500 of a list using `OFFSET`, which still computes and throws away every earlier row. Fixes come in layers. Make bounds part of the interface: require a time range, cap page size, and paginate with a keyset instead of OFFSET. Shape tables so that the bound prunes whole partitions. Keep old data small with retention policies and downsampled rollups. Then add guards that stop whatever slips through: PostgreSQL’s `statement_timeout` (off by default), ClickHouse’s `max_execution_time`, `max_rows_to_read` and `force_index_by_date`, and Prometheus’s `--query.timeout` and `--query.max-samples`.
analogy: Asking a librarian for “every book that mentions rain” instead of “this week’s weather reports”. The first request has no end, and it gets longer every time the library buys a book.
useWhen: An unbounded read is fine on a table that is small and stays small, such as countries or feature flags
One-off exports and backfills, run off-peak against a replica or snapshot, with a known cost
Batch jobs that read everything on purpose and stream rows instead of holding them all in memory
avoidWhen: Dashboards, APIs and anything a user can trigger again and again
Append-only data such as logs, events and metrics, which only grows
Shared databases, where one full scan slows every other query
Code that turns every returned row into an object in memory
example: A factory dashboard has a “units produced” panel running `SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE line_id = 4`. In the first month it reads 2 million rows and answers in 50 ms. Two years later the table holds 1.5 billion rows, the panel takes 40 seconds, and ten people opening the dashboard at the 8:00 shift change saturate the database’s disks. The fix has three parts: the panel gets `$__timeFilter(time)` so it reads only the range on screen, the all-time total moves to a daily continuous aggregate (730 rows for two years), and the dashboard’s database role gets `statement_timeout = '15s'`.

source: -- Unbounded: cost grows with every row ever written
SELECT * FROM events WHERE device_id = 7 ORDER BY time DESC;
-- Still unbounded: OFFSET computes and discards 100,000 rows first
SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100000;
-- Bounded: a time range lets the planner skip old partitions
-- Keyset pagination: continue after the last row already seen
-- A guard for whatever slips through, per role

diagram.caption: Two panels on one dashboard query the same events table. The live panel names a 15-minute range, so the database reads one recent partition and answers almost at once. The all-time panel names no range, so every partition is read and it answers far later, and it gets slower every day the table grows.

sections.title: Where it happens, and the guard

rows.label: PostgreSQL
values: No `WHERE` on time or key; a large `OFFSET`
Partition pruning on a time range; keyset pagination; `statement_timeout`, which is 0 (off) by default

rows.label: ClickHouse
values: A filter the primary key or date partition can’t use
`max_rows_to_read` and `max_execution_time` (throw, or break with a partial result); `force_index_by_date` and `force_primary_key` reject queries that can’t use the index

rows.label: Prometheus
values: A range query over months of raw samples
`--query.timeout` (2 minutes by default) and `--query.max-samples` (50 million by default)

rows.label: Grafana and Loki
values: A SQL panel without a time filter; a log query over a huge range
The `$__timeFilter()` macro; Loki’s `max_query_length` (30 days and 1 hour by default) and `max_query_series` (500)

rows.label: DynamoDB
values: `Scan`, which reads every item; filters apply after reading
`Query` by partition key instead; a Scan returns at most 1 MB per request, so it pages, and `Limit` caps items per page

rows.label: Cassandra
values: `ALLOW FILTERING`, which runs a full scan
A table designed for the query, so the partition key bounds it

story: In December 2007 Michael Nygard, author of Release It!, published that year, wrote about two clients with the same problem. A retailer’s checkout page took two minutes because one slot pulled thousands of matching products and turned each row into an object. At the second site, a query returned 1.2 million rows and ran for 90 seconds or more; the app server built objects until it ran out of memory, holding row locks that blocked every other server. He called it an “Unbounded Result Set” and gave the rule: “You should make your apps be paranoid about their data.” The second edition of Release It! (2018) still lists unbounded result sets among its stability antipatterns.

Pagination turned out to be the most common hiding place. Markus Winand’s 2014 post “We need tool support for keyset pagination” explained that `OFFSET` gives the database only a number of rows to throw away, so it must still fetch and sort them, and that pages shift when rows are inserted in between. His alternative, keyset pagination, continues from the last value seen.

Databases and monitoring tools then built in guardrails. Cassandra refuses queries that would scan every partition unless they say `ALLOW FILTERING`; DynamoDB returns at most 1 MB per Scan page; Prometheus aborts a query after 2 minutes or 50 million samples by default; Loki caps query length; ClickHouse has a family of complexity limits. PostgreSQL has `statement_timeout`, but it is off unless you set it.

choices.choice: Make bounds part of the interface
choices.why: An API that requires a time range and caps page size can’t be asked for everything by accident. A database can only see the query it is given.

OFFSET tells the database how many rows to discard, so it must produce them all first. A keyset (`WHERE id > last_seen`) lets an index start at the next page, and pages don’t shift when rows are inserted.
CQL rejects queries that would scan every partition unless the caller opts in, so the expensive path is visible in the code and in review.
A timeout doesn’t make a query cheaper; it stops one bad query from holding connections, memory and locks for everyone, which is how Nygard’s second client lost all its app servers.
